title: Climate change economics
content: Climate change economicsClimate change creates economic costs through changes in agriculture, health, infrastructure, productivity, and ecosystems. These effects are distributed unevenly across countries, regions, sectors, and households.Economic analysis can help compare mitigation and adaptation strategies and understand the incentives created by different policies. The long time horizon and uncertainty associated with climate change make these decisions particularly challenging.

title: Labour Codes
content: What India’s Labour Codes (2019–2020) Mean for the Worker.Article 2026In the summer of 2020, as millions of migrant workers walked home along highways emptied by the lockdown, Parliament was finishing the biggest rewrite of labour law since Independence. The timing was hard to ignore. The four Labour Codes on Wages (2019), and on Industrial Relations, Social Security, and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions (2020) merge twenty-nine central laws into four, and were finally brought into force on 21 November 2025, with central and state rules still being notified through 2026 (Ministry of Labour and Employment, 2025). They promise a simpler and more universal set of rights. The critical question is whether a reform designed largely around the registered factory can reach the workers on that highway: the self-recruited mason from Araria on a Surat construction site, the beautician sent out by an app, the young woman on a fixed-term contract in a Tiruppur garment unit.The Codes deserve a fair hearing. They act on the Second National Commission on Labour’s (2002) recommendation to consolidate a tangle of overlapping laws carrying a dozen odd competing definitions of “wages” into one coherent frame. The Code on Wages extends minimum-wage and timely-payment rights to every employee, ending the old confinement to “scheduled” employments, and its uniform wage definition, which caps excludable allowances at half of total remuneration, closes a loophole long used to suppress provident fund and gratuity liabilities. The Code on Social Security gives gig, platform and unorganised workers their first statutory recognition. The OSH Code widens “inter-state migrant worker” to include the self-recruited precisely the circular migrants the 1979 Act never found (Srivastava, 2020) and mandates appointment letters, annual health check-ups and a yearly journey allowance. Fixed-term workers gain benefit parity and pro-rata gratuity; women gain the right to night work with consent and safeguards. On paper, this is universalisation.Yet the architecture rests on thresholds, and thresholds are where inclusion quietly ends. The Industrial Relations Code raises the bar for prior government permission before retrenchment or closure from 100 to 300 workers, with power to lift it further by notification; standing orders now bind only establishments above 300; the OSH Code doubles the factory-size thresholds and raises the contract-labour trigger from 20 to 50 workers. In an economy where over 98 per cent of non-farm establishments employ fewer than ten people and roughly ninety per cent of workers are informally employed (PLFS, 2024), each raised threshold pushes more workers outside the law’s cover. The unprotected majority that the NCEUS (2007) documented two decades ago remains the norm, not the exception. Nor is the economics behind these moves as settled as the rhetoric implies: threshold-based regimes do distort firm-size choices (Amirapu and Gechter, 2020), but the “missing middle” they are meant to cure is itself hard to find in the data (Hsieh and Olken, 2014).The employment case for flexibilisation is thinner still. Besley and Burgess’s (2004) influential finding that pro-worker regulation depressed Indian manufacturing has been seriously qualified on measurement grounds (Bhattacharjea, 2006), and the natural experiments run by states after 2014 Rajasthan’s threshold amendments foremost produced no visible break in registered-manufacturing job creation (Sundar, 2019). What rigidity demonstrably produced was evasion: the contract-labour share of organised manufacturing employment roughly doubled between 2000 and 2015 (Kapoor and Krishnapriya, 2019). The Codes’ answer, statutory fixed-term employment, honestly legalises this reality and attaches benefits to it; but with no limit on successive renewals, it risks converting the permanent workforce into a rotating one rather than converting casual workers into secure ones. Flexibility may relax one margin of firm growth. It is not an employment strategy; demand, credit, infrastructure and skills bind far harder.The deeper worry concerns voice and security the two things a worker cannot purchase alone. The IR Code extends the fourteen-day strike notice once reserved for public utilities to every industrial establishment and counts concerted casual leave as a strike, narrowing lawful collective action in a country that has never ratified ILO Conventions 87 and 98 on freedom of association and collective bargaining. The Social Security Code, meanwhile, is written in enabling language: government “may” frame schemes for gig and platform workers, financed by an aggregator contribution of one to two per cent of turnover, capped at five per cent of payments to workers. Nothing is self-executing; the rights exist only if governments choose to act on them. The national floor wage has sat at Rs 178 a day since 2019 less than half the Rs 375 recommended by the government’s own expert committee (Satpathy Committee, 2019) while roughly a third of wage workers were already paid below the legal minimum before the Codes (ILO, 2018). Delivery capacity is not the constraint: e-Shram enrolled over thirty crore unorganised workers within four years, and the 2025 Union Budget extended Ayushman Bharat cover to registered gig workers. But registration is an address, not an entitlement. With NITI Aayog (2022) projecting 2.35 crore gig workers by 2029–30, and Rajasthan (2023) and Karnataka (2025) legislating ahead of the Centre, India risks a patchwork in which a delivery rider’s accident cover depends on where the algorithm sends her.Implementation will now decide the argument. Labour is a concurrent subject; the Codes took effect with most state rules unfinished, and by mid-2026 a majority of states had notified rules for at least one Code while others were still drafting, so the effective law a worker faces varies by border. The shift to “inspector-cum-facilitators”, randomised web-based inspections and compoundable offences may reduce the harassment of honest firms or hollow out deterrence in a system where under-enforcement, not over-regulation, has been most workers’ daily experience. Which of these happens is an empirical question, and an urgent one. The research agenda is straightforward: tracking the transitions of fixed-term and contract workers in successive PLFS rounds; auditing whether wages, bonuses and final dues actually arrive within the new timelines; linking e-Shram registration to realised benefits; and testing whether night-shift provisions raise women’s employment or merely their commuting risk.Any assessment has to end with the workers the law is meant to reach. The 2020 exodus exposed workers who held rights on paper and nothing in hand: nearly nine in ten stranded workers surveyed in the first weeks of lockdown had not been paid for work already done (SWAN, 2020). The Codes are best read as an unfinished bridge between paper rights and lived ones genuinely simpler, genuinely wider in aspiration, yet with their most universal promises left discretionary and their firmest protections reserved for a shrinking island of large formal establishments. Whether the mason from Araria ever crosses that bridge will depend less on the neatness of consolidation than on floor wages that are honest, schemes that are funded, inspections that happen, and unions that can still speak. That, and not the count of statutes repealed, is the standard by which the Labour Codes should be judged.References      Amirapu, A. and M. title: George Orwell
content: George OrwellGeorge Orwell was the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair (1903–1950), an English novelist, essayist, journalist, and critic. He was born in Motihari, India, and spent much of his early life in England.Before becoming a full-time writer, Orwell served as a police officer in Burma. His experiences there contributed to his opposition to imperialism and later informed some of his writing about colonialism and power.Orwell wrote extensively about poverty, war, political power, social inequality, language, and the relationship between individuals and institutions. His nonfiction includes Down and Out in Paris and London, The Road to Wigan Pier, and Homage to Catalonia.He is best known for Animal Farm (1945) and Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949). Animal Farm is a political satire about a revolution that develops into a new system of domination, while Nineteen Eighty-Four examines surveillance, political control, propaganda, and the manipulation of language. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}Orwell’s writing combined political and social commentary with a strong emphasis on clear and direct language. His essays and novels have continued to influence discussions of political power, freedom, propaganda, and the use of language in public life.

title: Vandana Shiva
content: Vandana ShivaVandana Shiva is an Indian environmental thinker, writer, activist, and scholar whose work focuses on ecology, agriculture, biodiversity, food systems, intellectual property, and the relationship between environmental change and social justice.She was trained as a physicist and completed a PhD in the philosophy of quantum theory at the University of Western Ontario. She later moved into interdisciplinary research on science, technology, environmental policy, and agriculture.In 1982, Shiva founded the Research Foundation for Science, Technology and Ecology. She later founded Navdanya, a movement focused on biodiversity conservation, seed sovereignty, and the rights of small farmers. Her work has also addressed the effects of agricultural technologies, patents, and industrial farming on farmers and local communities. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}Shiva is the author of numerous books, including Staying Alive, Monocultures of the Mind, Soil Not Oil, Who Really Feeds the World?, and The Violence of the Green Revolution. Her writing combines environmental analysis with arguments about agriculture, political economy, technology, and social change. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}The Violence of the Green Revolution: Third World Agriculture, Ecology and Politics, first published in 1991, examines the effects of Green Revolution agriculture in India. The book discusses monoculture, genetic diversity, chemical fertilizers, irrigation, soil fertility, and the social and political consequences of agricultural transformation, particularly in Punjab. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}Shiva has received numerous international awards for her work on environmental and social issues, including the Right Livelihood Award in 1993. She continues to work through Navdanya on biodiversity, seed conservation, ecological agriculture, and food sovereignty. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}

title: Jean Drèze
content: Jean DrèzeJean Drèze is a development economist whose research and writing focus on economic and social development, particularly in India. He has taught at the London School of Economics and the Delhi School of Economics and has been a Visiting Professor at Ranchi University.His work has examined a wide range of issues including poverty, hunger, nutrition, education, health care, employment, social security, and public policy. He has combined economic analysis with field research and close attention to the experiences of people affected by public programmes and social policies.Drèze has been closely associated with research and public discussion on India’s social policy. His work has contributed to debates around the right to food, employment guarantees, school meals, the public distribution system, health care, and elementary education.He is the co-author, with Amartya Sen, of Hunger and Public Action and An Uncertain Glory: India and Its Contradictions. He is also the author of Sense and Solidarity: Jholawala Economics for Everyone, which brings together essays on social development and public policy in India. (Oxford Academic)Sense and Solidarity discusses issues including poverty, school meals, health care, child development, employment guarantees, food security, the public distribution system, corporate power, and social policy. The book also argues for an approach to development economics in which research, practical experience, and democratic action are closely connected. (Oxford Academic)Drèze’s work has therefore combined economic research with field experience and engagement with questions of social policy, public institutions, and the conditions of everyday life.

title: Rukmini S.
content: Rukmini S.Rukmini S. is a data journalist and author based in Chennai. She is the founder and director of Data for India, a public platform focused on making data and information about India more accessible and useful to researchers, policymakers, and the wider public.She began her journalism career covering Mumbai for the Times of India and later specialised in data journalism. She was the first Data Editor at The Hindu and subsequently worked as Editor for Data and Innovation at HuffPost India. Her work combines statistical analysis with field reporting and an interest in understanding what official data can and cannot reveal about people’s lives.Her work focuses particularly on demographics, gender, household economics, inequality, caste, and politics. She has also written extensively about India’s statistical systems and the interpretation of social and economic data. Her reporting has appeared in publications including Mint, IndiaSpend, The Guardian, and other Indian news organisations. (Data for India)Rukmini is the author of Whole Numbers and Half Truths: What Data Can and Cannot Tell Us About Modern India, published by Westland in 2021. The book uses official statistics, surveys, field reporting, and other evidence to examine how India is changing and where commonly used numbers can give an incomplete or misleading picture of society. (Google Books)Her work has received several awards, including recognition at the Sigma Awards for Data Journalism and the Asian College of Journalism Awards. Her pandemic reporting and analysis of India’s COVID-19 data also received recognition from health and policy communities. (NALSAR University of Law)Her approach to journalism emphasises the importance of understanding the context behind statistics. Rather than treating numbers as self-explanatory, her work examines how data are collected, what they measure, what they leave out, and how they can shape public understanding of India.

title: J. W. Mason
content: J. W. MasonJ. W. Mason is an economist whose research focuses on macroeconomics, finance, economic history, and the distribution of economic power. He is an Associate Professor of Economics at John Jay College, City University of New York.His work examines questions about investment, financial institutions, corporate decision-making, and the way economic power shapes macroeconomic outcomes. He has also written extensively for a wider public audience on economics and economic policy.Mason is the co-author, with Arjun Jayadev, of Against Money. Their work examines the role of money, finance, and economic institutions and questions some conventional ways of thinking about financial markets and economic policy.His writing combines economic theory with historical and institutional analysis, with an emphasis on understanding how economic systems actually operate rather than treating markets as separate from political and institutional structures.

title: Arjun Jayadev
content: Arjun JayadevArjun Jayadev is a Professor of Economics at Azim Premji University in Bengaluru and Director of the Centre for the Study of the Indian Economy. He is also a Senior Economist at the Institute for New Economic Thinking.He previously taught Economics at the University of Massachusetts, Boston and was an inaugural post-doctoral fellow at Columbia University’s Committee on Global Thought. He holds a PhD in Economics from the University of Massachusetts, Amherst.His research interests include international economics, economics of distribution, political economy, macroeconomic dynamics, and the economics of power. His research combines quantitative and theoretical approaches to questions involving finance, development, political economy, and intellectual property.Jayadev has written extensively on income and wealth distribution, financial systems, labour, macroeconomic policy, inequality, and the distributional consequences of financial institutions. He has also worked on questions involving household debt, financial reform, interest rates, and macroeconomic policy.He has collaborated extensively with J. W. Mason on research concerning household debt, financial systems, macroeconomic policy, and distribution. He is the co-author of Against Money.

title: Arundhati Roy
content: Arundhati RoyArundhati Roy is an Indian writer whose work spans fiction, essays, political writing, and memoir. Her first novel, The God of Small Things, was published in 1997 and won the Booker Prize that year. Her second novel, The Ministry of Utmost Happiness, was published in 2017 and was longlisted for the Booker Prize. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}Roy has also written extensively on politics, society, inequality, democracy, conflict, and contemporary India. Her nonfiction includes The End of Imagination, The Algebra of Infinite Justice, Field Notes on Democracy, Broken Republic, Capitalism: A Ghost Story, The Doctor and the Saint, My Seditious Heart, and Azadi. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}Her writing often combines literary essays with political and social commentary. Her nonfiction has addressed questions of power, state institutions, inequality, violence, democracy, and the effects of political and economic change.In 2023, Roy received the European Essay Prize for lifetime achievement, and in 2024 she received the PEN Pinter Prize. She lives in Delhi. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}Her memoir Mother Mary Comes to Me, published in 2025, explores her relationship with her mother, Mary Roy, and traces how her childhood, family life, and experiences shaped her development as a writer. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}

title: James C. Scott
content: James C. ScottJames C. Scott (1936–2024) was an American political scientist and anthropologist whose work focused on political economy, agrarian societies, peasant politics, state power, resistance, and Southeast Asia. He was a professor at Yale University, where he held appointments in political science, anthropology, and environmental studies. He also founded and directed Yale’s Program in Agrarian Studies. (yale.edu)Scott’s research was strongly grounded in fieldwork and historical analysis. His work examined how ordinary people respond to systems of political and economic power, including the ways in which peasants and other subordinate groups resist, negotiate with, or adapt to state authority and social hierarchies.His major books include The Moral Economy of the Peasant, Weapons of the Weak, Domination and the Arts of Resistance, Seeing Like a State, The Art of Not Being Governed, and Against the Grain. His research crossed the boundaries of political science, anthropology, history, geography, and development studies. (yale.edu)Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed, first published in 1998, examined why large-scale state planning can fail when governments simplify complex societies and environments in order to make them easier to administer. The book emphasizes the importance of local, practical knowledge that may be lost when centralized schemes impose standardized systems. (Yale University Press)Scott’s later work extended these interests to questions of state formation, agriculture, political autonomy, and societies that remained relatively outside the control of centralized states. His scholarship had a wide influence across the social sciences, particularly in studies of development, governance, agrarian change, and political resistance.

title: M. R. Sharan
content: M. R. SharanM. R. Sharan is an economist and researcher whose work focuses on development economics, political economy, governance, and public policy in India. His research examines how state institutions, public programmes, and local political structures shape the lives and opportunities of people, particularly in rural areas.His work has included research on bureaucracy, governance, poverty alleviation, and Panchayati Raj institutions. He has also worked extensively with field-based data and research methods to understand how public institutions function on the ground.Sharan is the author of Last Among Equals: Power, Caste and Politics in Bihar’s Villages, published in 2021. The book examines village politics in Bihar through the interaction of caste, power, local institutions, and political change.His research combines economic analysis with detailed field research, with particular attention to the relationship between formal institutions and the social and political structures within which they operate.

title: Milton Friedman
content: Milton FriedmanMilton Friedman (1912–2006) was an American economist and one of the leading figures in twentieth-century monetary economics. He taught at the University of Chicago from 1946 to 1976 and later served as a senior research fellow at the Hoover Institution. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}Friedman received the 1976 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his contributions to consumption analysis, monetary history and theory, and his analysis of stabilization policy. His work made important contributions to monetary economics, including the study of the relationship between money supply, economic activity, and inflation. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}He became closely associated with the Chicago School of economics and was an influential advocate of monetary explanations of inflation and economic fluctuations. His research also covered consumption, business cycles, monetary policy, and international economics. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}Friedman also wrote extensively for a wider audience about economic policy and individual freedom. His books include Capitalism and Freedom, written with Rose D. Friedman and first published in 1962, and Free to Choose, also written with Rose Friedman. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}Capitalism and Freedom discusses the relationship between economic and political freedom and covers subjects including monetary policy, fiscal policy, international trade, education, inequality, and poverty. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
