title: Starting with a research question
content: Starting with a research questionA research project begins with a question that can be stated clearly enough to guide the collection and analysis of evidence. A useful question identifies the outcome of interest, the relevant population or setting, and the relationship that the researcher wants to understand.The question also determines what kind of data and research design are appropriate. Spending time refining the question before beginning analysis can prevent large amounts of work on data or methods that do not answer the underlying research problem.

title: Writing reproducible code
content: Writing reproducible codeReproducible code should take clearly defined inputs and produce outputs through a documented sequence of operations. Scripts should be organised so that another researcher can understand the order in which cleaning, analysis, and output generation occur.Readable code is also easier to debug and modify. Consistent naming, modular functions, comments, and clear folder structures can make empirical research substantially easier to maintain.

title: Documenting research decisions
content: Documenting research decisionsResearch projects involve many decisions about data construction, variable definitions, exclusions, coding, and analysis. If these decisions are not recorded, it becomes difficult to understand why the final results look the way they do.Documentation can take the form of code comments, readme files, data dictionaries, research notes, and version controlled scripts. The goal is to make the reasoning behind the analysis recoverable.

title: Checking data quality
content: Checking data qualityData quality checks are designed to identify errors before the dataset is used for analysis. These checks can include missingness, ranges, duplicates, inconsistent identifiers, unexpected categories, and relationships between variables that should logically hold.Quality checks should be repeated after major transformations. Automated checks are particularly useful because they can be rerun whenever the data or cleaning code changes.

title: Managing research files
content: Managing research filesResearch projects can quickly accumulate raw data, cleaned datasets, scripts, documents, figures, and intermediate outputs. A clear folder structure helps prevent confusion between original files and files created during analysis.File names should be descriptive and consistent. Important files should also be backed up and changes should be tracked so that earlier versions can be recovered when necessary.

title: Finding and organising the literature
content: Finding and organising the literatureA literature review helps establish what is already known about a research question and where important gaps remain. It involves identifying relevant theoretical arguments, empirical findings, datasets, and methodological approaches.Organising the literature systematically makes it easier to compare studies and identify differences in questions, settings, data, and identification strategies. Good notes should capture the main contribution of a study as well as the assumptions behind its conclusions.

title: Building a research dataset
content: Building a research datasetBuilding a research dataset involves bringing together information from one or more sources and creating variables that correspond to the research question. This can involve merging files, constructing identifiers, transforming variables, and adding geographic or administrative information.A useful dataset should retain information about where each variable came from and how it was constructed. Keeping raw files separate from processed data makes it easier to reproduce the analysis and identify errors.

title: From analysis to research writing
content: From analysis to research writingResearch writing connects the empirical analysis to the question that motivated the project. The results should be presented in a way that makes the identification strategy, evidence, and limitations understandable to the reader.Writing can also reveal weaknesses in the analysis. Explaining what a coefficient means, why a comparison is credible, and what alternative explanations remain can help identify areas where additional analysis is needed.

title: Creating tables and figures
content: Creating tables and figuresTables and figures should communicate the main empirical patterns clearly. They should have informative labels, consistent definitions, and enough information for the reader to understand what is being presented.Generating outputs through code helps ensure consistency across revisions. It also makes it easier to update tables and figures when the underlying dataset or analysis changes.

title: Cleaning raw data
content: Cleaning raw dataData cleaning involves identifying missing values, duplicates, inconsistent formats, impossible values, and other problems in raw information. The process should be based on an understanding of how the data were collected rather than simply changing unusual observations.Every important cleaning decision should be documented. Original values should be preserved where possible so that changes can be checked and revised if new information becomes available.

title: Randomized Controlled Trials
content: Randomized Controlled TrialsA Randomized Controlled Trial assigns individuals, households, schools, firms, or other units to different groups using a random process. Random assignment helps ensure that treatment and comparison groups are similar on average before the intervention takes place.The difference in outcomes between the groups can then provide evidence about the causal effect of the intervention. Careful implementation remains important because attrition, noncompliance, spillovers, and measurement problems can affect the interpretation of experimental results.

title: Understanding the PLFS sampling design
content: Understanding the PLFS sampling designThe PLFS uses a complex sampling design rather than a simple random sample of individuals. Households are selected through multiple stages, and the design incorporates geographical units, stratification, and sampling probabilities. Understanding these stages is necessary for interpreting estimates correctly.Survey weights allow observations in the sample to represent the wider population from which they were selected. Researchers also need to account for clustering and stratification when estimating standard errors. Ignoring these features can produce misleading measures of precision.

title: Working with messy government data
content: Working with messy government dataGovernment datasets often contain inconsistent formats, missing values, duplicate records, changing variable names, and administrative terminology that is difficult to interpret. These problems are common when data are assembled from different offices or collected over long periods.Working with such data requires a systematic cleaning process. The researcher needs to understand how the data were generated, document every transformation, preserve the original files, and create checks that identify unexpected changes. Good data cleaning is therefore part of the research process rather than a purely technical exercise.

title: Constructing historical geographic crosswalks
content: Constructing historical geographic crosswalksHistorical geographic crosswalks allow researchers to translate information from one set of administrative boundaries into another. They are particularly useful when datasets collected in different periods use different district or constituency boundaries.A crosswalk can be constructed using geographic overlap between historical and current polygons. The resulting relationship can then be represented either as a dominant match or as shares of the source area associated with different target units. The choice depends on the research question and the information available.

title: Periodic Labour Force Survey
content: Periodic Labour Force SurveyThe Periodic Labour Force Survey is an important source for studying employment, unemployment, labour force participation, and the structure of work in India. It provides information about the labour market characteristics of individuals and households and allows researchers to examine differences across states, demographic groups, and types of employment.Working with the PLFS requires careful attention to the survey structure, variables, weights, and definitions used to classify labour market activity. The data can be used to study employment patterns, unemployment, labour force participation, wages, migration, and differences between rural and urban labour markets.

title: SurveyCTO and field data collection
content: SurveyCTO and field data collectionSurveyCTO can be used to program questionnaires, collect responses electronically, implement skip patterns, and monitor fieldwork. Digital data collection can reduce some forms of manual data entry and allow researchers to build validation rules directly into the survey instrument.The quality of the final dataset still depends on field implementation. Enumerator training, pilot testing, regular checks, and careful monitoring are necessary to identify problems while data collection is taking place rather than after the survey has ended.

title: Working with spatial data in R
content: Working with spatial data in RR provides a flexible environment for working with geographic data. Spatial objects can be read, transformed, joined, intersected, and visualised within a reproducible workflow. This makes it possible to combine administrative records with geographic boundaries and coordinate data.Spatial analysis also requires attention to coordinate reference systems. Distances, areas, intersections, and maps can produce incorrect results when geographic objects use incompatible systems. A careful workflow therefore checks projections and geometry before performing spatial operations.

title: Working with QGIS
content: Working with QGISQGIS is useful for inspecting, cleaning, joining, and visualising spatial data. It provides a graphical environment in which geographic boundaries, points, and other spatial layers can be examined directly. This is especially useful when checking the results of geocoding or spatial matching.QGIS can also support research workflows that combine visual inspection with statistical analysis. Researchers can identify unusual locations, examine boundary changes, verify geographic relationships, and prepare spatial files before taking them into R or another statistical environment.

title: Experimental research in development economics
content: Experimental research in development economicsExperimental research in development economics studies how policies, institutions, information, and incentives affect economic behaviour. Researchers can use experiments to test specific mechanisms and estimate the effects of interventions in real world settings.Good experimental research begins with a clearly defined question and a credible design. The researcher must also consider implementation, measurement, ethical issues, statistical power, and whether the setting allows the findings to be applied to other populations or contexts.

title: The redesigned PLFS from 2025
content: The redesigned PLFS from 2025The redesigned PLFS from 2025 changes important aspects of the survey structure and data collection system. Understanding these changes is necessary when working with the newer rounds because variables, schedules, sampling arrangements, and the organisation of the unit level data may differ from earlier versions.Researchers using the redesigned survey need to distinguish changes in the underlying labour market from changes introduced by the survey redesign. Careful documentation of variables and survey concepts is therefore important when comparing the new data with earlier rounds.

title: Building an India district panel
content: Building an India district panelAn India district panel brings together information on districts across multiple years so that changes in economic, social, demographic, and institutional conditions can be studied over time. Constructing such a panel requires identifying which geographic units correspond to one another in different periods.The main difficulty is that district boundaries change over time. New districts can be created, existing districts can be divided, and names can change. A useful panel therefore requires a systematic geographic crosswalk rather than simply matching district names across datasets.

title: Geocoding schools and administrative records
content: Geocoding schools and administrative recordsGeocoding converts names and addresses into geographic coordinates that can be used for spatial analysis. Administrative datasets often contain locations in inconsistent formats, making automated geocoding difficult. Names may contain spelling differences, abbreviations, missing information, or historical place names.A reliable geocoding workflow therefore combines automated services with cleaning and validation. Results can be checked using geographic boundaries, nearby locations, postal information, and alternative sources. Records that cannot be confidently matched should remain identifiable as unresolved rather than being assigned arbitrary coordinates.

title: Matching names across datasets
content: Matching names across datasetsMatching names across datasets is often necessary when there is no common identifier. Names can differ because of spelling variations, abbreviations, punctuation, changes in language, or differences in how an institution or location is recorded.A good matching process combines automated standardisation with manual validation. Exact matches can be handled first, followed by increasingly flexible matching methods. Ambiguous matches should be reviewed rather than automatically accepted because an incorrect match can introduce serious errors into the final dataset.

title: Building reproducible research workflows
content: Building reproducible research workflowsA reproducible research workflow makes it possible to understand how raw data were transformed into the results presented in a research project. This requires organised files, documented code, consistent naming conventions, and clear separation between raw data and processed outputs.Reproducibility also reduces the risk of errors during repeated analysis. When cleaning, analysis, tables, and figures are generated through documented scripts, changes can be made systematically and the same analysis can be rerun when new data or corrections become available.

title: Matching districts across Census years
content: Matching districts across Census yearsDistrict names cannot always be used directly to match administrative units across Census years. A district may have the same name but different boundaries, while two different names may refer to areas that later become part of the same district.Matching districts therefore requires combining names, geographic boundaries, codes, and information about district creation and division. The objective is to establish a consistent relationship between geographic units while preserving information about changes in administrative boundaries.

title: Survey design and questionnaire development
content: Survey design and questionnaire developmentA survey questionnaire translates a research question into measurable variables. Good questionnaire design requires deciding what information is necessary, how questions should be worded, what response options should be available, and how questions should be ordered.Poorly designed questions can introduce measurement error even when data collection is implemented correctly. Piloting helps identify confusing wording, missing response categories, inappropriate skip patterns, and questions that respondents find difficult to answer.

title: Difference in Differences
content: Difference in DifferencesDifference in Differences is a method for estimating the effect of an intervention by comparing changes over time between a treated group and a comparison group. The central idea is that the change experienced by the comparison group provides information about what might have happened to the treated group without the intervention.The credibility of the method depends heavily on the assumptions behind the comparison. One important condition is that the groups would have followed similar trends in the absence of treatment. Researchers therefore examine pre treatment trends and carefully define the treatment, comparison group, and time periods.

title: Pilot surveys and enumerator training
content: Pilot surveys and enumerator trainingA pilot survey provides an opportunity to test the questionnaire and field procedures before the main data collection begins. It can reveal problems with question wording, survey length, respondent understanding, sampling procedures, and technical implementation.Enumerator training is equally important because the way a question is presented can affect the response. Training should establish consistent procedures while preparing enumerators to handle questions, unexpected situations, consent, and data quality issues during fieldwork.

title: Cleaning and standardising administrative data
content: Cleaning and standardising administrative dataAdministrative datasets are often collected for operational purposes rather than research. As a result, the same organisation, office, designation, or location may appear in many different forms. Cleaning requires identifying these variations and developing consistent representations.Standardisation should preserve the original information while creating variables that can be used reliably for analysis. A useful workflow keeps raw values unchanged, documents transformations, and creates standardised variables separately so that every change remains traceable.

title: Survey weights and complex survey design
content: Survey weights and complex survey designSurvey weights account for differences in the probability that observations are selected into a sample. They allow researchers to construct estimates that better represent the population covered by the survey. Weights can arise from sampling probabilities, nonresponse adjustments, and other features of survey design.Weights are only one part of a complex survey design. Clustering and stratification can also affect the calculation of standard errors. Researchers therefore need to understand the complete survey design rather than applying weights without considering how the sample was constructed.

title: Extracting information from PDFs
content: Extracting information from PDFsMany government records and historical documents are distributed as PDF files rather than structured datasets. Extracting information from these documents can involve identifying tables, reading text, handling scanned pages, and preserving the relationship between different parts of a document.Automated extraction can greatly reduce repetitive work, but extracted information needs to be checked against the original documents. Tables can be misread, characters can be confused, and scanned documents may require additional processing. Validation is therefore essential when building a research dataset from PDFs.

title: Building analysis ready survey data
content: Building analysis ready survey dataRaw survey data usually require several stages of preparation before they can be used for analysis. These stages can include checking identifiers, cleaning variables, handling missing values, verifying skip patterns, constructing derived measures, and checking the consistency of responses.The goal is to create a dataset in which every analytical variable has a clear definition and a reproducible construction process. Good survey data preparation also involves maintaining documentation so that another researcher can understand how the final variables were produced.

title: Research data and replication
content: Research data and replicationResearch data should be organised so that the origin and transformation of each analytical variable can be understood. This includes maintaining information about source files, cleaning procedures, variable definitions, and the code used to produce analytical datasets.Replication requires more than making a final dataset available. A researcher should also provide sufficient information about the construction of the data and the analytical procedure for another researcher to understand how the reported results were produced. Good documentation is therefore a central part of empirical research.

title: Data and Methods
content: Data and methodsNotes on the datasets and empirical tools that I use in research.Periodic Labour Force SurveyThe Periodic Labour Force Survey is an important source for studying employment and labour market conditions in India. It provides information on labour force participation, employment, unemployment, workers, household characteristics, and different forms of economic activity. I use the survey to understand patterns in labour markets across individuals, households, and regions.Working with PLFS requires more than simply opening the data and running regressions. The questionnaire, variable definitions, coding structure, missing values, sampling design, and survey weights all need to be understood before analysis. I therefore treat the documentation and structure of the survey as an important part of the empirical work.The redesigned PLFS from 2025The redesigned PLFS introduced from 2025 provides a new framework for collecting and reporting information on labour market conditions in India. The changes are important for researchers because the frequency and organisation of the survey affect how labour market indicators can be studied over time.The redesigned survey also requires care when comparing recent observations with earlier PLFS rounds. Changes in questionnaires, sampling procedures, definitions, and estimation methods can influence measured outcomes. Understanding these changes is necessary before making comparisons across different periods.Understanding the PLFS sampling designUnderstanding the sampling design is an important part of working with household survey data. PLFS observations come from a structured sample rather than a simple random selection of individuals. The sample design determines how households enter the survey and how observations should be interpreted in relation to the wider population.Sampling weights, strata, and sampling clusters can affect both estimates and statistical inference. I therefore try to understand how the sample was constructed before calculating population statistics or estimating relationships. This helps ensure that the empirical analysis reflects the design of the survey.Building an India district panelAn India district panel can be used to study economic and social changes across geographic areas over time. District level data can provide a useful way to examine differences in development, employment, public services, infrastructure, and other outcomes across regions.Building such a panel is not simply a matter of combining files from different years. District boundaries and administrative structures change over time, and new districts are created from older ones. Constructing a consistent panel therefore requires careful geographic matching and documentation of the decisions used to connect observations across years.Matching districts across Census yearsDistricts in India have changed substantially across different Census periods. A district recorded in one Census may later be divided into several districts, merged with another area, or renamed. This creates difficulties when attempting to compare district level outcomes across different Census years.I approach this as a geographic matching problem rather than relying only on district names. Historical boundaries, administrative changes, geographic locations, and other information can help determine how observations from different periods should be connected. Keeping the original identifiers is also important for checking the resulting matches.Constructing historical geographic crosswalksHistorical geographic crosswalks provide a way to connect geographic units that were defined differently at different points in time. They are particularly useful when combining datasets collected under different administrative boundaries. Without a crosswalk, apparently similar geographic observations may not actually represent the same area.Constructing a crosswalk requires decisions about how older and newer geographic units overlap. Geographic boundaries, area relationships, and population information can all be useful depending on the research question. I also find it important to document the original geographic units and the procedures used to create the final relationship.Geocoding schools and administrative recordsMany administrative datasets contain names and addresses but do not provide reliable geographic coordinates. Geocoding converts these descriptions into geographic locations that can be used for mapping and spatial analysis. This is particularly useful for schools, government offices, villages, and other public institutions.Geocoding is also a data quality problem. A returned coordinate does not automatically mean that the observation has been correctly located. Names need to be standardised, possible matches need to be examined, and selected observations often need additional verification before the coordinates can be used confidently.Working with spatial data in RR provides a useful environment for combining data cleaning with spatial analysis. Spatial data can be used to map observations, connect points to administrative boundaries, calculate distances, and examine geographic patterns. Keeping these operations within a coded workflow also makes the analysis easier to reproduce.I use spatial workflows when research questions require information about where observations are located. Repeated geographic operations can be automated through code rather than performed manually for every dataset. This becomes especially useful when working with large numbers of schools, districts, villages, or administrative records.Working with QGISQGIS is useful for visually examining geographic data. Maps can reveal problems that may not be obvious when looking at a table of coordinates or administrative identifiers. Incorrect locations, unusual clusters, boundary problems, and unexpected geographic patterns can often be identified through visual inspection.I see QGIS as complementary to statistical programming. Code is useful for performing the same operation systematically across a large dataset, while QGIS is useful for examining the results visually. Moving between the two can make spatial data cleaning and validation more reliable.Cleaning and standardising administrative dataAdministrative data often contain substantial variation in names, formats, categories, and identifiers. The same institution, office, designation, or location can appear differently across different files. These differences can create problems when several administrative sources need to be combined.I prefer to preserve the original values while creating standardised versions for analysis. This makes it possible to trace a cleaned observation back to its original form. Standardisation should make the dataset easier to analyse while keeping the cleaning process transparent and verifiable.Matching names across datasetsMatching names across datasets is often more difficult than it appears. Names may differ because of spelling, punctuation, abbreviations, spacing, transliteration, or changes in official terminology. Two records that look different may refer to the same entity, while similar names may refer to different entities.I use a combination of standardisation, exact matching, approximate matching, and manual verification. Approximate matching can help identify possible matches, but it should generally be treated as a way of generating candidates rather than as final evidence. Additional information is often necessary to establish whether two records genuinely refer to the same entity.Working with messy government dataGovernment datasets can contain valuable information that would be difficult to collect independently. At the same time, these datasets may contain inconsistent formats, missing identifiers, duplicate observations, changing classifications, and limited documentation. Working with them therefore requires substantial attention before they can be used for empirical analysis.I try to understand how the data were originally produced before making extensive changes to them. This includes examining the source, structure, definitions, identifiers, and patterns of missing information. The cleaning process should preserve enough information to explain how the original records were transformed into the final research dataset.Extracting information from PDFsPDF documents often contain useful information that is not available in machine readable datasets. Government reports, administrative records, tables, lists, and historical documents may all need to be extracted before they can be used in quantitative research.Extraction itself does not guarantee accurate data. Tables can be incorrectly read, scanned documents can produce recognition errors, and formatting can be lost during conversion. I therefore treat extracted information as an intermediate product that needs to be checked against the original document before being incorporated into a research dataset.Building analysis ready survey dataSurvey data usually require substantial preparation before they can be used for analysis. Variables may have unclear names, different coding systems, missing value codes, multiple questionnaire versions, and derived measures that need to be constructed. Understanding the questionnaire is therefore an important part of understanding the dataset.I treat cleaning as part of the research process rather than as a purely technical step. Decisions about missing observations, sample restrictions, variable construction, and coding can affect empirical results. Keeping these decisions documented makes the movement from raw survey data to analysis ready data easier to understand.Survey weights and complex survey designHousehold surveys are generally designed to provide information about a wider population rather than only the people who were interviewed. Survey weights help account for the way observations were selected and allow researchers to produce estimates that correspond more closely to the population represented by the survey.Weights are only one component of a complex survey design. Stratification and clustering can also affect estimation and standard errors. I therefore try to understand the complete survey design before deciding how a dataset should be analysed rather than treating the weight variable as an ordinary variable.Difference in DifferencesDifference in Differences is a method for studying changes associated with an intervention or policy when some units are exposed to the intervention and others are not. The basic comparison considers how outcomes change over time for the treated group relative to the change experienced by a comparison group.The credibility of the approach depends heavily on the research design. In particular, researchers need to think carefully about whether the comparison group provides a reasonable representation of what would have happened to the treated group without the intervention. Timing, pre intervention trends, anticipation, and other simultaneous changes can therefore be important.Randomized Controlled TrialsRandomized Controlled Trials use a random process to assign participants or other units to different groups. Random assignment is intended to create comparable groups before an intervention takes place. Differences in outcomes between the groups can then provide evidence about the effect of the intervention.The statistical idea is only one part of an experiment. Recruitment, randomisation, treatment delivery, measurement, attrition, and survey implementation can all influence the quality of the final evidence. Careful preparation and monitoring during fieldwork are therefore essential parts of experimental research.Experimental research in development economicsExperimental research can be used to study whether specific interventions affect economic and social outcomes. In development economics, experiments have been used to examine questions involving education, employment, information, public services, financial decisions, health, and household behaviour.I am particularly interested in the connection between the research question, intervention, and outcome being measured. An experiment requires decisions about who participates, how treatment is delivered, what information is collected, and how outcomes are measured. Good experimental research therefore combines economic reasoning with careful field implementation and empirical analysis.Survey design and questionnaire developmentA questionnaire is the main instrument through which many research projects measure behaviour, beliefs, experiences, and outcomes. The wording of questions, order of sections, response options, and length of an interview can all affect the information respondents provide.Questionnaire development therefore involves repeated testing and revision. Pilot interviews can reveal questions that respondents interpret differently from what the researcher intended, as well as response categories that do not capture common answers. Revising the questionnaire after testing can improve both measurement and the fieldwork process.SurveyCTO and field data collectionSurveyCTO allows researchers to conduct digital surveys using structured questionnaires with skip patterns, validation rules, calculations, and other controls. These features can reduce some common data entry problems and make it possible to organise field data in a consistent format.Good digital data collection still depends on the people implementing the survey. Enumerators need appropriate training, the questionnaire needs to be piloted, and submitted interviews need to be reviewed. I am interested in using digital survey tools to prevent avoidable errors while maintaining checks for unusual or unexpected observations.Pilot surveys and enumerator trainingA pilot survey provides an opportunity to understand how a questionnaire works under actual interview conditions. It can reveal how long interviews take, which questions are difficult to understand, whether response categories are appropriate, and where additional instructions are required.Enumerator training is closely connected to the pilot process. Enumerators need to understand the purpose of questions while asking them consistently and without influencing respondents. Reviewing pilot interviews and discussing problems before the main survey can improve both implementation and data quality.Building reproducible research workflowsA reproducible research workflow should make it possible to understand how a final result was produced from the original inputs. This involves keeping raw and processed data separate, organising scripts clearly, documenting transformations, and maintaining a record of changes to code and research files.I find this especially important when research involves repeated cleaning or several people working with the same data. A well organised workflow reduces the risk of losing files or forgetting how a result was produced. It also makes it easier to return to a project and understand the decisions that were made earlier.Research data and replicationReplication requires a clear path from the original data to the reported results. A researcher should be able to understand what data were used, what transformations were performed, and how the final tables or figures were generated. Clear documentation is therefore important even when the original data cannot be made publicly available.For my own work, this means keeping track of source files, cleaning scripts, intermediate datasets, and final outputs. I also find basic checks useful before finalising an analysis, including sample sizes, missing values, summary statistics, merge results, and consistency between the underlying data and reported results.

title: What Makes a Job a Good Job?
content: What Makes a Job a Good Job?A job is more than the wage attached to it. Workers may care about whether they are paid on time, whether the employer treats them respectfully, how predictable the work is, and whether they can rely on the employer to honour promises. These features can be particularly important in informal labour markets where formal contracts provide limited protection.Thinking about job quality from the worker’s perspective also changes how we think about labour-market matching. Two jobs with similar wages may not be equally attractive if their working conditions are very different. I find this useful for thinking about both worker choices and the incentives firms face when trying to attract and retain workers.

title: State Capacity and Everyday Public Services
content: State Capacity and Everyday Public ServicesState capacity is often discussed in terms of taxation, law enforcement, or the ability of governments to implement large policies. But capacity is also visible in much smaller interactions: whether a public institution has the resources it needs, whether records are maintained, whether staff are present, and whether a policy actually reaches the people it is intended to serve.Fieldwork has made me interested in this gap between policy on paper and implementation on the ground. Looking closely at local institutions can reveal administrative constraints that are difficult to see in aggregate data. It also raises questions about how budgets, incentives, information, and accountability interact in the delivery of public services.

title: Trust, Information, and Civic Engagement
content: Trust, Information, and Civic EngagementCitizens often have to make decisions about government without having complete information about what public institutions are doing. They may know that a programme exists without knowing how it works, who is eligible, or whether implementation has taken place in their area. The quality and accessibility of information can therefore shape how people perceive and interact with the state.This makes trust an interesting outcome to study. Better information may increase confidence when government performance matches what citizens are told, but it may also change perceptions when people discover gaps between policy and implementation. I am interested in this relationship between information, trust, and civic engagement.

title: Information Frictions in Labour Markets
content: Information Frictions in Labour MarketsMarkets work differently when people do not have complete information. A worker looking for a job may not know which employers pay on time, provide reasonable working conditions, or keep their promises. Similarly, an employer may have limited information about a worker’s skills, reliability, or previous experience.These information gaps can affect who meets whom in the labour market and which jobs workers accept. They can also create a role for information-sharing institutions, recommendations, networks, or other mechanisms that help workers and firms make better decisions. This is one reason I find information frictions useful for thinking about informal employment and migration.

title: Why Is Informal Work So Persistent?
content: Why Is Informal Work So Persistent?Informal work is not simply a temporary stage on the way to a formal job. For many workers, informal employment is a long-term way of earning a living. Workers may value the flexibility of informal work, while employers may value the lower fixed costs and flexibility that informal arrangements provide. At the same time, workers can face limited social protection, uncertain incomes, and weak bargaining power.This makes informality an interesting development question. I am interested in understanding when informal employment reflects a worker’s choice, when it reflects a lack of alternatives, and how firms and institutions shape these decisions. Looking at informality through both the worker and employer side seems particularly useful for understanding India’s labour market.

title: Can Better Information Change How Citizens Engage with Government?
content: Can Better Information Change How Citizens Engage with Government?Giving people information is often assumed to improve their ability to participate in public life. But information has to be understandable, credible, and relevant before it can affect behaviour. A citizen may receive a detailed explanation of a government programme but still be unable to use it if the information is difficult to interpret or does not answer the questions that matter to them.Generative AI makes this question particularly interesting. AI systems can potentially turn complicated administrative information into simpler explanations, but they also create concerns about accuracy and interpretation. I am interested in whether the format in which government information is presented can affect trust, understanding, and civic engagement.

title: Public-Sector Employment and the Search for Government Jobs
content: Public-Sector Employment and the Search for Government JobsGovernment employment is an important part of the aspirations of many young workers in India. Public-sector jobs can offer relatively predictable employment, wages, benefits, and social status. At the same time, recruitment processes can involve substantial competition, repeated examinations, long preparation periods, and uncertainty about when vacancies will become available.I am interested in the behaviour of people who spend considerable time preparing for public-sector employment. The search process itself raises questions about information, expectations, opportunity costs, and how people respond to uncertainty. Understanding these choices can tell us something about labour-market allocation as well as the broader demand for secure employment.

title: Tourism, Employment, and Mountain Economies
content: Tourism, Employment, and Mountain EconomiesTourism can be an important source of employment in mountain regions, but its effects are not uniform. It can create demand for accommodation, transport, food, construction, and local services while also increasing pressure on land, infrastructure, water, and other resources. The interesting question is therefore not simply whether tourism creates jobs, but what kinds of jobs it creates and who benefits from them.Mountain economies also face geographic constraints that shape how local economies develop. Remoteness can make some activities expensive while making natural and cultural amenities economically valuable. I am interested in how tourism interacts with local labour markets, migration decisions, household livelihoods, and the broader development of mountain regions.

title: Labour Markets in India
content: Labour Markets in IndiaIndia’s labour market is interesting partly because the same economy contains very different kinds of work. A worker may have a regular salaried job, work as a casual labourer, run a small household enterprise, or combine several activities across the year. This makes simple measures of employment difficult to interpret. I am particularly interested in how workers move between these forms of employment, how wages and working conditions differ across them, and how local economic opportunities shape these choices.The Periodic Labour Force Survey provides an important starting point for studying these questions because it allows us to look at employment, unemployment, labour-force participation, and the characteristics of workers and their jobs. I am interested in the relationship between informality, migration, urbanisation, and development, and in understanding the constraints that shape the choices workers make.

title: Why Do Firms Hire Migrant Workers?
content: Why Do Firms Hire Migrant Workers?Hiring decisions are usually discussed from the perspective of workers, but firms also have preferences over whom they employ. Employers may care about reliability, skills, previous experience, wage demands, and whether workers are likely to remain in the job. These considerations can become especially important in informal labour markets where contracts and formal screening mechanisms are limited.Migrant workers can also face an information disadvantage. They may know less about local employers and working conditions, while employers may know less about workers’ backgrounds. Understanding these information gaps can help explain why workers and firms sometimes make decisions that look surprising from the outside.

title: Climate, Migration, and Local Labour Markets
content: Climate, Migration, and Local Labour MarketsClimate and weather shocks can affect labour markets through several channels. A poor agricultural season can reduce household income and demand for local labour, while extreme weather can damage homes, infrastructure, and productive assets. Households may respond by changing how much they work, what activities they undertake, or whether someone migrates.This makes migration one possible way households respond to economic and environmental shocks. But migration itself has costs, and the ability to move may depend on credit, social networks, information, and opportunities at the destination. I am interested in how environmental shocks interact with these constraints and shape labour-market decisions.

title: Development Questions in the Himalayan Region
content: Development Questions in the Himalayan RegionMountain regions face a particular combination of economic opportunities and geographic constraints. Distance from major markets, difficult terrain, limited connectivity, and exposure to environmental risks can affect access to jobs, education, healthcare, and markets. At the same time, tourism, agriculture, natural resources, and migration create important sources of income.I am interested in the Himalayan region partly because development cannot be understood separately from geography. Migration can connect mountain households to opportunities elsewhere, while tourism and local services can create employment closer to home. These interactions raise broader questions about regional inequality, public infrastructure, and the future of mountain economies.

title: Why Do Workers Migrate?
content: Why Do Workers Migrate?Migration is often described as a response to differences in wages and employment opportunities, but the decision to migrate is rarely that simple. Households also consider the cost of moving, access to information, family responsibilities, social networks, housing, credit, and the risks associated with finding work in another place.This makes migration closely connected to other areas of development economics. A change in rural employment opportunities, access to credit, public works, or local infrastructure can potentially affect whether people move. I am interested in how these constraints interact and how migration changes both the places workers leave and the places where they work.

title: Courses and training
content: Courses and trainingCourses and training provide a structured way to build knowledge in economic theory, empirical methods, and specialised research areas. I use them to strengthen foundations in development economics, labour economics, political economy, environmental economics, and quantitative methods.Training is particularly useful when it connects theoretical concepts with empirical applications. Working through research papers, datasets, problem sets, and applied exercises helps turn concepts into practical research skills.

title: Research collaborations
content: Research collaborationsResearch collaboration allows different researchers to contribute complementary skills, knowledge, and perspectives to a project. Collaboration can involve research design, data construction, fieldwork, empirical analysis, and writing.Working across projects has also provided opportunities to learn different approaches to empirical research. These experiences have strengthened my interest in development economics and applied research.

title: Academic milestones
content: Academic milestonesAcademic work develops through a sequence of education, research assistance, fieldwork, data analysis, and independent research. Each stage contributes different skills and helps shape the questions that I want to study.This section records important developments in that process. The purpose is to maintain a simple record of research related activities, rather than to provide a conventional curriculum vitae.

title: Fieldwork
content: FieldworkFieldwork provides an opportunity to understand how institutions, markets, and policies operate in practice. Interviews, surveys, observations, and conversations with participants can reveal information that may not be visible in administrative or survey datasets alone.Good fieldwork requires careful preparation and documentation. Questionnaire design, enumerator training, consent, piloting, data quality checks, and field protocols all influence the quality of the resulting evidence.

title: Research projects
content: Research projectsResearch projects bring together questions, data, methods, and institutional settings into a structured empirical investigation. My interests include development economics, labour markets, public institutions, migration, and environmental questions.Projects often evolve as new data and field evidence become available. I use this space to keep track of the research questions, empirical work, and ideas that are developing across different projects.

title: Climate change and development
content: Climate change and developmentClimate change can affect development through agricultural productivity, health, infrastructure, migration, and local employment. These effects are often particularly important for households whose livelihoods depend directly on environmental conditions.Adaptation can reduce some of these risks, but the ability to adapt differs across households and locations. Economic resources, public infrastructure, information, and institutional support can all influence how communities respond to climate change.

title: State capacity and development
content: State capacity and developmentState capacity concerns the ability of governments to collect information, implement policies, raise revenue, enforce rules, and provide public services. These functions are central to the functioning of modern economies and can affect development outcomes directly.Capacity is not uniform across governments or even within the same government. Local institutions, frontline workers, administrative systems, and available resources can all influence how effectively policies are implemented.

title: Technology and development
content: Technology and developmentTechnology can change productivity, reduce transaction costs, create new forms of employment, and alter access to information. Its effects can therefore extend across firms, households, markets, and public institutions.Technological change does not necessarily benefit everyone equally. Access to infrastructure, skills, finance, and information can determine who is able to adopt new technologies and who may be left behind.

title: Institutions and economic development
content: Institutions and economic developmentInstitutions shape the incentives faced by households, firms, and governments. Rules concerning property, contracts, taxation, political participation, and public administration can influence how economic decisions are made and how resources are allocated.Institutional differences can therefore help explain why economies with similar resources can experience different development outcomes. Studying institutions requires attention to both formal rules and the informal practices through which those rules operate.

title: Environment and economic development
content: Environment and economic developmentEconomic activity depends on natural resources and environmental systems, while production and consumption can also create pollution and other environmental costs. Development policy therefore involves choices about how resources are used and how environmental damages are managed.Environmental problems often involve externalities because the costs created by one person’s actions can affect others. Understanding these problems requires combining economic incentives with information about environmental conditions and institutional capacity.

title: Markets and development
content: Markets and developmentMarkets coordinate decisions made by households and firms through prices and exchange. In developing economies, markets can expand access to goods, employment, finance, and technology, but they may also function imperfectly because information and infrastructure are limited.Understanding development therefore requires examining both the benefits of markets and the conditions required for markets to work well. Transaction costs, market power, missing markets, and information problems can all affect economic outcomes.

title: Education and human capital
content: Education and human capitalEducation can increase knowledge, skills, productivity, and access to employment opportunities. Human capital is therefore an important component of economic development and can affect both individual earnings and broader economic outcomes.The effects of education depend on the quality and relevance of learning as well as years of schooling. Access, school quality, teacher availability, and household circumstances can all influence whether additional schooling translates into improved outcomes.

title: Health and development
content: Health and developmentHealth affects people’s ability to work, study, participate in economic activity, and live productive lives. Poor health can reduce household income while also creating substantial expenditure on treatment and care.Health outcomes are influenced by income, nutrition, sanitation, healthcare access, environmental conditions, and public institutions. Development analysis therefore needs to consider health both as an outcome and as an important input into economic wellbeing.

title: Political economy and development
content: Political economy and developmentPolitical economy studies how political institutions and economic interests interact. Policies are not determined only by their technical economic effects because different groups can gain or lose from policy choices.This perspective helps explain why economically beneficial reforms may be difficult to implement. Political incentives, distributional conflicts, institutions, and collective action can all influence policy decisions.

title: Migration and development
content: Migration and developmentMigration can be an important mechanism through which households respond to differences in economic opportunities across locations. Workers may move temporarily or permanently in response to wages, employment opportunities, household needs, or economic shocks.Migration can affect both origin and destination economies. Remittances can support households in origin areas, while migrant workers can contribute labour to destination economies. The effects depend on the characteristics of migrants and the institutions through which migration takes place.

title: Labour markets and development
content: Labour markets and developmentLabour markets connect workers who supply their time and skills with firms and other organisations that demand labour. In developing economies, these markets are often divided across formal and informal employment and across agriculture, manufacturing, construction, and services.Changes in labour markets are closely connected to structural transformation. As economies develop, workers may move across sectors, occupations, locations, and types of employment, creating important consequences for productivity, wages, and household welfare.

title: Amartya Sen and development
content: Amartya Sen and developmentAmartya Sen’s work provides a way of thinking about development that goes beyond income and economic growth. Development can be understood in terms of the expansion of people’s capabilities and their ability to lead lives that they have reason to value.This perspective places freedom, opportunity, health, education, and access to resources at the centre of development analysis. It also highlights why economic development cannot be evaluated only through aggregate income or production.

title: Firms and development
content: Firms and developmentFirms play a central role in employment, productivity, investment, innovation, and structural transformation. Differences in firm size, management, technology, finance, and market access can affect economic outcomes.Development economics therefore increasingly studies firms directly. Understanding employer behaviour can help explain hiring, productivity, worker outcomes, and the expansion or survival of enterprises.

title: Social protection
content: Social protectionSocial protection policies aim to reduce economic insecurity and protect households against shocks. They can include transfers, insurance, pensions, employment programmes, and other forms of public support.Studying social protection involves examining both coverage and effects. Important questions include who receives benefits, how programmes affect household behaviour, and whether administrative systems successfully reach intended beneficiaries.

title: Education and development
content: Education and developmentEducation can affect productivity, earnings, health, social mobility, and economic growth. Development research therefore studies both access to education and the quality of learning that students receive.Important questions include how families make schooling decisions, how schools produce learning, and which policies improve educational outcomes. These questions often involve household constraints, teacher incentives, school resources, and institutional design.

title: Labour economics
content: Labour economicsLabour economics studies how workers and firms make decisions about employment, wages, skills, and job search. It also examines institutions such as labour regulations, unions, contracts, and social protection.The subject provides tools for understanding unemployment, wage differences, migration, human capital, labour supply, and employer behaviour. These topics are closely connected to development and public policy.

title: Private enterprise development
content: Private enterprise developmentPrivate firms can contribute to development through employment, investment, innovation, and the production of goods and services. Small firms in low income settings often face constraints involving finance, technology, management, and market access.Research in this area studies which constraints matter most and whether interventions can improve firm performance. Understanding firm behaviour is important for designing policies aimed at productivity and employment.

title: Environmental economics
content: Environmental economicsEnvironmental economics studies how economic decisions affect environmental resources and how policy can address environmental problems. Pollution and resource depletion often create costs that are not fully reflected in market prices.The field therefore examines instruments such as taxes, regulation, property rights, and markets for environmental services. It also considers how environmental benefits and costs can be measured and valued.

title: Industrial organisation
content: Industrial organisationIndustrial organisation studies how firms compete and how market structure affects prices, entry, innovation, and consumer outcomes. It examines markets in which firms have some degree of market power.The field provides tools for analysing competition, monopolies, oligopolies, product differentiation, and regulation. These concepts are useful for understanding how firms behave when markets are not perfectly competitive.

title: Structural transformation and economic growth
content: Structural transformation and economic growthStructural transformation concerns changes in the sectoral composition of an economy as productivity and incomes rise. Workers and resources may move from agriculture into manufacturing and services, although the pattern differs across countries.The process is closely connected to productivity growth, urbanisation, migration, and changes in labour demand. Understanding why transformation occurs at different speeds is an important development economics question.

title: Urban economics
content: Urban economicsUrban economics studies how people and firms locate across cities and how economic activity is organised spatially. Housing, transportation, land markets, agglomeration, and local public services are central topics.Cities can generate productivity benefits because firms and workers interact more frequently in dense locations. At the same time, congestion, housing costs, pollution, and unequal access to services can create important urban challenges.

title: Political economy
content: Political economyPolitical economy studies how political institutions and economic incentives shape policy and economic outcomes. It is useful for understanding why policies differ across settings and why economically desirable reforms may face political constraints.The subject also connects distributional consequences with political behaviour. Studying who gains and who loses from a policy can help explain political support, opposition, institutional persistence, and the implementation of reforms.

title: Development economics
content: Development economicsDevelopment economics studies how economies and living standards change over time and why outcomes differ across people and places. It covers questions involving poverty, education, health, labour markets, firms, institutions, and public policy.Modern development economics combines economic theory with empirical research. Household surveys, administrative data, field experiments, and other methods are used to understand mechanisms and evaluate interventions.

title: Uncontrolled Tourism
content: Uncontrolled tourism leads to the loss of intellectual property.Article 2026India’s mountainous regions, such as Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and the northeastern states, are unable to provide employment opportunities commensurate with the growing aspirations of their residents due to difficult geographical conditions. However, these snow-capped mountains are crucial for tourism. Tourism Department data shows that domestic tourism has increased significantly in recent decades (Ministry of Tourism, Government of India, 2022). With the exception of a few states, almost all mountainous states saw 70 to 188% more domestic tourist arrivals in 2021 compared to 2020 (Ministry of Tourism, Government of India, 2022; Kaushik & Thakur, 2024). Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh saw increases of approximately 350 and 4394%, respectively (Ministry of Tourism, Government of India, 2022). This growth is driven by political efforts and government provision of infrastructure such as roads. The rise in domestic tourism is also an indicator of the country’s growing economic prosperity, as only with economic stability can the population afford to spend on luxuries like tourism.Although the mountains cannot attract large factories and industries, these same mountain ranges attract tourists and bring economic prosperity to the plains for their residents. However, mountainous regions pay a heavy price for promoting tourism (Capocchi et al., 2019). Scenic tourism relies on modern amenities such as roads, internet, ropeways, resorts, hotels, and waste management, and a breakdown in any of these facilities adversely impacts the tourist experience. Small towns like Manali and Kullu host approximately three to six times their permanent population each year, yet the massive volume of waste generated by these tourists is simply too large to handle in their waste management systems (Census of India, 2011; The Tribune, 2024a, 2024b). Consequently, heaps of garbage can often be seen along the banks of rivers and their tributaries (Nüsser et al., n.d.; Down To Earth, 2026). Thus, deforestation for roads and a lack of waste management destroy the very beauty that attracts tourists to the mountains.The negative impact of tourism based solely on superficial natural beauty has also been seen on education and social intelligence. The 2021 National Achievement Survey conducted by the Department of School Education and Literacy revealed a decline in the quality of education in almost all mountainous regions (National Council of Educational Research and Training, 2021; Press Trust of India, 2025). While this decline may be due to many reasons, economists consider the decline in educational quality in states like Himachal Pradesh to be a symptom of “Dutch Disease” (Corden & Neary, 1982; Corden, 1984). Dutch disease is not a physical or mental illness, but rather refers to the disruption of development in another region caused by sudden economic growth in a specific region (Corden & Neary, 1982). Therefore, when tourism increases, it often draws resources, such as skilled labor, from other industries (Alkhathlan et al., 2019).In India, over the past two decades, due to economic stability, improved infrastructure, and social media, tourism in mountainous regions has seen a significant boom, attracting and engaging rural youth. Indian mountainous regions attract tourists with their natural beauty. Unlike European nations, mountainous states have failed to attract domestic tourists with the cultural and historical heritage displayed in museums. States like Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, and Himachal Pradesh attract religious tourists due to the presence of some prominent temples, but their numbers are extremely low. Social media is also dominated by novel and exotic experiences. A very small segment of people visit the mountains to experience the unique traditions, culture, and lifestyle, and out of positive curiosity. Most trekking is conducted in the name of eco-tourism (Sati, 2018; Kuniyal et al., 2025). When quick money can be earned with a few hours of hard work, by becoming a tour guide, selling two-minute noodles at exorbitant prices, by drug trafficking, or by trekking, why would anyone pay for years of study? The lack of skilled labor due to the lack of higher education also impacts other industries. In many areas, tourism fuels inflation, forcing local citizens, who are the custodians of cultural heritage, to migrate (Mikulić et al., 2021; Mamgain & Reddy, 2018; Milano et al., 2019). The recent anti-tourism protests in Italy are indicative of this (Barry, 2024; Euronews with Associated Press, 2024; Wilson, 2025). There’s no doubt that mountain tourism is crucial and should be promoted. However, the growth of this industry needs to be managed very carefully. If mountain tourism relies not only on natural observation but also on the local culture and historical heritage, young people should study culture and history in universities. A tour guide should not only sell the crafts and handicrafts of their state but also understand the history behind them, their social significance, and their uniqueness, thus spreading knowledge. When a tourist wanders in an environment rich in knowledge, they will think twice before littering.While the government is building roads, airports, and ropeways, it should also ensure that libraries and museums are built to preserve and teach folk art and knowledge, and make them so attractive that tourists are drawn there. As tourists learn about local culture, they will ask more questions of the tour guide and trekker, and the answers will be found in books and in the company of wise and learned people.References      Alkhathlan, K., Alkhareif, R., & Barnett, W.
