title: Psychology and economics
content: Psychology and economicsPsychology and economics studies how human behaviour differs from the assumptions of standard economic models. Attention, beliefs, preferences, limited information, and behavioural biases can influence economic decisions.The field can help explain choices involving saving, education, health, labour supply, and public policy. Behavioural insights can also inform the design of interventions intended to improve individual or social outcomes.

title: Migration and development
content: Migration and developmentMigration is closely connected to differences in labour demand, wages, household resources, and economic opportunities. It can change the allocation of workers across regions and sectors and affect both migrants and their families.Research on migration also considers the costs of moving and the role of networks and information. These factors can determine who migrates, where people move, and what kinds of employment they obtain.

title: Why Do Firms Hire Migrant Workers?
content: Why Do Firms Hire Migrant Workers?Research InternCentre for the Study of the Indian Economy (CSIE), Azim Premji UniversityPatna, BiharJune–July 2025Supervisor: Prof. Chinmaya Kumar (Azim Premji University, Bengaluru)FieldworkWorked on Why Do Firms Hire Migrant Workers?, a cross-randomized field experiment examining employer hiring preferences in informal labor markets.Assisted and supervised 5 enumerators during the pilot survey and facilitated interviews with 25 construction contractors and 15 households to collect primary data using SurveyCTO.Assisted with questionnaire design and piloting, reviewed and refined enumerator training materials, trained 5 enumerators, and conducted audio audits for data quality during implementation.

title: What is state capacity?
content: What is state capacity?State capacity is the ability of public institutions to perform core functions such as raising revenue, enforcing rules, collecting information, and delivering public services. It can vary across countries, regions, agencies, and levels of government.Strong administrative systems can make it easier to implement policies consistently. Weak capacity can create gaps between policies as written and the services or outcomes experienced by citizens.

title: What is omitted variable bias?
content: What is omitted variable bias?Omitted variable bias occurs when an important variable is left out of a regression and that variable is related both to the outcome and to an included explanatory variable. The coefficient on the included variable can then capture part of the effect of the omitted factor.The direction and size of omitted variable bias depend on the relationships among the variables. Adding controls can reduce the problem when the controls are appropriate, but researchers need to consider whether the additional variables themselves are affected by the treatment or outcome.

title: What is spatial inequality?
content: What is spatial inequality?Spatial inequality refers to differences in economic and social outcomes across geographic areas. Regions can differ in income, employment, education, health, infrastructure, public services, and access to markets.These differences can persist because geography interacts with institutions, historical development, investment, migration, and economic opportunities. Studying spatial inequality therefore requires attention to both local conditions and broader economic processes.

title: What is survey weighting?
content: What is survey weighting?Survey weighting assigns different importance to observations so that the sample can represent the population from which it was drawn. An observation that represents many people in the population receives a larger weight than an observation representing fewer people.Weights are determined by the survey design and may also incorporate adjustments for nonresponse or other factors. Using the correct weights is important when estimating population level quantities from complex surveys.

title: What are information frictions?
content: What are information frictions?Information frictions occur when people do not have complete or accurate information when making economic decisions. Workers may not know about available jobs, firms may not know the characteristics of applicants, and consumers may not know the quality of products.These frictions can prevent mutually beneficial exchanges from occurring. Networks, information platforms, search mechanisms, and public disclosure can sometimes reduce the costs created by incomplete information.

title: What are fixed effects?
content: What are fixed effects?Fixed effects allow researchers to account for unobserved characteristics that are constant within a unit over time. For example, a panel dataset can use individual fixed effects to remove time invariant differences between individuals.Fixed effects can be useful when those unobserved characteristics are correlated with explanatory variables. They do not, however, solve every source of omitted variable bias because characteristics that change over time remain relevant.

title: What is a Randomized Controlled Trial?
content: What is a Randomized Controlled Trial?A Randomized Controlled Trial assigns units to treatment and comparison groups through a random process. Because assignment is random, differences between groups after the intervention can be interpreted as causal under appropriate implementation conditions.Randomization does not automatically guarantee a successful experiment. Attrition, noncompliance, spillovers, weak implementation, and measurement problems can affect the estimated treatment effect. These issues must therefore be considered when interpreting experimental results.

title: What is an externality?
content: What is an externality?An externality occurs when an action by one person or firm affects the welfare of another person without that effect being fully reflected in the market price. Pollution is a common example because production can impose costs on people who are not directly involved in the transaction.Externalities can lead to inefficient outcomes because private decisions do not account for the full social costs or benefits. Policy responses can include taxes, regulation, property rights, or other institutional arrangements.

title: What is structural transformation?
content: What is structural transformation?Structural transformation describes the movement of labour and economic activity across sectors as an economy develops. A common pattern involves declining agricultural employment and increasing activity in manufacturing and services.The process can raise productivity when workers move into more productive activities. The pace and form of transformation differ across countries and depend on technology, trade, institutions, education, infrastructure, and labour demand.

title: Why does migration happen?
content: Why does migration happen?Migration can occur because economic opportunities differ across locations. Differences in wages, employment, education, public services, and living conditions can create incentives to move.People also face costs when they migrate. Travel, housing, information, social networks, uncertainty, and family responsibilities can all affect whether a person is able or willing to move.

title: What is human capital?
content: What is human capital?Human capital refers to knowledge, skills, health, and other characteristics that affect a person’s productivity and economic opportunities. Education and training are common ways through which human capital can be accumulated.Human capital can affect earnings, employment, productivity, and economic growth. Its effects depend not only on the quantity of education or training but also on quality and how well skills match available economic opportunities.

title: What is Difference in Differences?
content: What is Difference in Differences?Difference in Differences compares changes in outcomes over time between a treated group and a comparison group. The comparison is based on the idea that the comparison group can provide information about the change that would have occurred for the treated group without the intervention.The key identifying assumption is that the groups would have followed similar trends in the absence of treatment. Researchers therefore pay close attention to pre treatment trends and to whether other events affected the groups differently.

title: What is political economy?
content: What is political economy?Political economy studies how political institutions, incentives, and economic interests interact. It asks how policies are chosen and how political arrangements influence economic outcomes.A political economy approach recognises that policies create distributional consequences. Different groups may have different preferences over taxation, regulation, public spending, and institutional change, creating conflicts over policy.

title: What is internal migration?
content: What is internal migration?Internal migration occurs when people move from one location to another within the same country. The movement can be temporary, seasonal, circular, or permanent and can occur for employment, education, family reasons, or other purposes.Internal migration connects local labour markets and can redistribute workers across regions and sectors. Understanding it requires attention to both origin and destination conditions as well as the costs associated with moving.

title: What is a public good?
content: What is a public good?A public good is typically defined by non rivalry and non excludability. Non rivalry means that one person’s use does not reduce the amount available to others, while non excludability means that it is difficult to prevent people from using the good.These characteristics can create problems for private provision because individuals may have incentives to benefit without contributing to the cost. Public goods therefore provide an important setting for studying collective action and government intervention.

title: What is labour market informality?
content: What is labour market informality?Labour market informality refers to employment relationships that operate outside some formal institutional arrangements. Informal workers may lack written contracts, social protection, regulated working conditions, or other features associated with formal employment.Informality can arise from many sources, including firm size, regulation, enforcement, productivity, worker characteristics, and labour market institutions. It is therefore useful to examine the specific form of informality rather than treating all informal employment as identical.

title: What is a carbon market?
content: What is a carbon market?A carbon market creates a system in which emissions or emissions reductions are assigned an economic value. Depending on the design, firms may trade permits or credits associated with greenhouse gas emissions or reductions.The objective is to create incentives for reducing emissions while allowing flexibility in how reductions are achieved. The effectiveness of a carbon market depends on measurement, monitoring, enforcement, market design, and the credibility of the underlying emissions units.

title: What is climate adaptation?
content: What is climate adaptation?Climate adaptation refers to actions that reduce the harm caused by current or expected climate impacts. Households, firms, communities, and governments can adapt through changes in infrastructure, technology, behaviour, land use, and public policy.Adaptation opportunities differ across locations and households. Access to finance, information, infrastructure, technology, and public institutions can determine how effectively people respond to climate related risks.

title: What is a sampling frame?
content: What is a sampling frame?A sampling frame is the list or structure from which units are selected into a sample. It may contain households, individuals, firms, schools, geographic areas, or other units depending on the research design.The quality of a sampling frame affects the quality of the resulting sample. Missing units, duplicates, outdated information, and systematic coverage differences can create problems even when the sampling procedure itself is correctly implemented.

title: What is the Coase Theorem?
content: What is the Coase Theorem?The Coase Theorem describes a setting in which parties affected by an externality can potentially reach an efficient outcome through bargaining when property rights are clearly defined and transaction costs are sufficiently low.The result highlights the importance of transaction costs and institutions. In real world settings, bargaining may be difficult because many affected parties are involved, information is incomplete, or negotiating and enforcing agreements is costly.

title: What is selection bias?
content: What is selection bias?Selection bias occurs when the units observed in one group differ systematically from the units observed in another group in ways that matter for the outcome. A simple comparison can then combine the effect of the treatment with pre existing differences between groups.Random assignment is one way to reduce selection bias because treatment status is determined independently of potential outcomes. In observational research, researchers need alternative strategies to address differences between treated and comparison groups.

title: What is causal inference?
content: What is causal inference?Causal inference asks what would happen to the same unit under different possible conditions. The central challenge is that researchers cannot normally observe both the treated and untreated outcome for the same unit at the same time.Research designs attempt to construct credible comparisons that approximate this missing counterfactual. Experiments, natural experiments, Difference in Differences, instrumental variables, and other methods use different assumptions to address this problem.

title: Economics Explainers
content: Economics explainersShort explanations of concepts that come up repeatedly in my coursework and research.What is Difference in Differences?Difference in Differences is a method used to study changes in outcomes associated with an intervention, policy, or event. It compares the change over time for a group affected by the intervention with the change over time for a comparison group that was not affected. The method is useful when researchers want to estimate a causal effect using observational or quasi experimental data.The central idea is to compare differences rather than simply comparing groups or periods. A major assumption is that, in the absence of the intervention, the treated and comparison groups would have followed similar trends over time. Researchers therefore need to examine the research setting, timing, treatment exposure, and underlying trends carefully.What is a Randomized Controlled Trial?A Randomized Controlled Trial is an experimental research design in which individuals, households, firms, communities, or other units are randomly assigned to different groups. Usually, one group receives an intervention while another group serves as a comparison. Random assignment helps ensure that the groups are comparable before the intervention begins.The difference in outcomes between the groups can then provide evidence about the effect of the intervention. In practice, however, an experiment involves much more than random assignment. Recruitment, treatment delivery, survey implementation, attrition, measurement, and compliance can all affect the quality of the evidence.What is causal inference?Causal inference is the study of whether a particular intervention, exposure, or change actually causes a change in an outcome. This is different from simply identifying a correlation between two variables. For example, observing that education and earnings are positively related does not by itself establish that additional education causes higher earnings.The central challenge is the counterfactual. Researchers want to know what would have happened to the same unit under a different treatment or exposure. Since both outcomes cannot normally be observed for the same unit at the same time, empirical methods attempt to construct credible comparisons that approximate the missing counterfactual.What is selection bias?Selection bias occurs when the units included in an analysis differ systematically from the population or comparison group that the researcher wants to study. The problem can arise when participation, treatment assignment, survey response, or inclusion in a dataset is related to characteristics that also affect the outcome.Selection bias can make a relationship appear stronger, weaker, or even opposite to the relationship that exists in the broader population. Researchers therefore need to understand how observations entered the sample and whether the process of selection is related to the variables being studied.What is omitted variable bias?Omitted variable bias occurs when an important variable is left out of a statistical model and that variable is related both to the explanatory variable of interest and to the outcome. In such a situation, the estimated relationship can partly capture the effect of the omitted factor rather than the relationship that the researcher is trying to measure.For example, suppose education is related to earnings and ability affects both education and earnings. If ability is not adequately accounted for, the estimated relationship between education and earnings may reflect both education and differences in ability. The problem is therefore closely connected to causal interpretation.What are fixed effects?Fixed effects are commonly used in panel data analysis to account for characteristics of observational units that do not change over time. For example, when studying individuals, firms, districts, or schools over several periods, some characteristics of those units may remain relatively stable but still affect the outcome.Including fixed effects allows the analysis to focus on variation within the relevant unit rather than relying entirely on differences between units. This can help account for unobserved time invariant characteristics, although fixed effects do not automatically solve every source of omitted variable bias or establish causality.What is survey weighting?Survey weighting is a method used to account for differences in the probability that observations are selected into a survey. Some people or households may have a higher probability of selection than others, and weights can be used so that the resulting estimates better represent the population from which the sample was drawn.Weights need to be interpreted together with the broader survey design. Stratification, clustering, nonresponse, and other features of the sampling process can also affect estimation. Applying a weight mechanically without understanding how it was constructed can therefore lead to incorrect conclusions.What is a sampling frame?A sampling frame is the underlying list, map, register, or other structure used to identify the population from which a sample is selected. It provides the practical basis for deciding which units can enter a survey. Depending on the study, the sampling frame might consist of households, individuals, villages, firms, schools, or other units.The quality of a sampling frame matters because gaps or errors in the frame can affect who has a chance of being selected. If important parts of the target population are missing, the resulting sample may not adequately represent the population that the researcher intends to study.What is internal migration?Internal migration refers to movement of people from one location to another within the same country. In India, this can involve movement between villages, towns, cities, districts, or states. People may move temporarily, seasonally, or for longer periods depending on employment, education, household circumstances, social networks, and other factors.Migration is therefore not a single phenomenon with one explanation. Different forms of migration can have different economic consequences for workers and households. Studying internal migration requires attention to the reasons for movement, the duration of migration, the destination, and the labour market conditions faced by migrants.Why does migration happen?Migration can occur because people expect better economic opportunities in another location. Differences in wages, employment opportunities, education, public services, household conditions, and local economic conditions can all influence migration decisions. Social networks can also reduce the costs and risks associated with moving.Migration decisions are often made within households rather than by individuals acting completely independently. People may move to diversify household income, support family members, respond to seasonal employment opportunities, or invest in education and future earnings. The reasons for migration can therefore vary substantially across workers and places.What is labour market informality?Labour market informality refers to economic activity and employment arrangements that operate outside some formal institutional structures and protections. Informal workers may have limited access to written contracts, social security, employment protections, or other forms of formal labour regulation.Informality is widespread and can take many forms. Workers may be employed by informal firms, work without formal contracts within otherwise formal organisations, or operate independently. Understanding informality therefore requires looking at both workers and firms and at the institutional environment in which employment takes place.What is human capital?Human capital refers to the knowledge, skills, health, abilities, and other characteristics that can affect an individual’s productivity and economic opportunities. Education and training are common examples, but human capital is broader than formal schooling alone. Health and accumulated work experience can also influence what people are able to do.Human capital is important in development economics because differences in skills, health, and knowledge can contribute to differences in productivity and earnings. Investments in education, training, health, and early childhood development can therefore affect both individual outcomes and broader economic development.What is structural transformation?Structural transformation refers to changes in the composition of an economy as development progresses. Historically, many economies have experienced a movement of workers and economic activity from agriculture toward manufacturing and services, accompanied by changes in productivity, urbanisation, and employment.The process is not identical across countries. The timing and scale of transformation depend on technology, trade, institutions, infrastructure, human capital, and labour markets. Understanding structural transformation therefore requires examining how sectors change and how workers and firms respond to those changes.What is state capacity?State capacity refers broadly to the ability of public institutions to implement policies, provide services, collect information, raise revenue, enforce rules, and carry out administrative functions. Capacity can vary across governments, departments, regions, and levels of administration.State capacity is important because policies depend not only on their formal design but also on implementation. A programme may have clearly defined objectives but produce different outcomes if administrative systems have difficulty identifying beneficiaries, delivering services, maintaining records, or monitoring implementation.What is political economy?Political economy studies how political institutions, incentives, power, and economic interests interact to shape policies and economic outcomes. It asks not only what a particular policy does but also why certain policies are adopted, how institutions influence decisions, and how different groups affect the allocation of resources.Political economy can be useful for understanding outcomes that cannot be explained solely by market forces or technical policy design. Institutions, political incentives, collective action, information, and distributional conflicts can all influence economic decisions and the implementation of public policy.What are information frictions?Information frictions arise when people do not have complete, accurate, or easily accessible information. In labour markets, workers may not know which firms are hiring or what wages different employers offer, while firms may have limited information about potential workers and their characteristics.These information gaps can affect decisions even when suitable opportunities exist. Workers may remain in low productivity employment, firms may have difficulty finding suitable employees, and transactions may take longer or involve greater search costs. Information can therefore influence labour market outcomes independently of wages and skills.What is a public good?A public good is a good or service with characteristics that make it difficult to exclude people from using it and where one person’s use does not necessarily reduce the amount available to others. National defence and some forms of public information are commonly used as examples.Public goods create a challenge for markets because individuals may have incentives to benefit from the good without contributing to its provision. This can result in under provision when decisions are left entirely to private markets. The characteristics of the good and the institutional setting determine the extent of this problem.What is an externality?An externality occurs when an action by one person, household, or firm affects another person’s welfare or production without that effect being fully reflected in the market transaction. Pollution is a common example because production or consumption can impose costs on people who are not directly involved in the transaction.Externalities can lead to inefficient outcomes when private decisions do not account for the full social costs or benefits of an activity. Policy responses can include taxes, subsidies, regulation, property rights, information, or other institutional arrangements depending on the nature of the external effect.What is the Coase Theorem?The Coase Theorem is an idea in economics concerning how parties affected by an externality may negotiate over the allocation of resources. Under highly restrictive conditions, including well defined property rights and very low transaction costs, bargaining can lead parties to an efficient outcome regardless of the initial allocation of rights.The conditions are important because real world transactions often involve significant costs. Information problems, bargaining costs, enforcement difficulties, large numbers of affected parties, and unequal access to resources can all make private negotiation difficult. The theorem is therefore useful for understanding the role of transaction costs and institutions.What is a carbon market?A carbon market is a system in which rights or obligations associated with greenhouse gas emissions can be traded. Depending on the design, participants may buy and sell emissions allowances or credits associated with reductions or removals of emissions.The basic economic idea is to attach a price to emissions so that firms and other actors face incentives to reduce pollution. The effectiveness of a carbon market depends on its institutional design, including how emissions are measured, how permits or credits are allocated, how compliance is monitored, and how the market is regulated.What is climate adaptation?Climate adaptation refers to actions that reduce the harmful effects of climate change or help people, communities, firms, and ecosystems adjust to changing environmental conditions. Examples include changes in agricultural practices, infrastructure investment, water management, disaster preparedness, and changes in where economic activities are located.Adaptation decisions involve both economic and social considerations. Different households and communities have different resources and constraints, which means their ability to respond to climate risks can vary. Understanding adaptation therefore requires attention to income, institutions, information, infrastructure, technology, and local environmental conditions.What is spatial inequality?Spatial inequality refers to differences in economic and social conditions across geographic areas. These differences can occur between states, districts, rural and urban areas, neighbourhoods, or other geographic units. Income, employment, education, health, infrastructure, and access to public services can all vary across space.Spatial inequality is important because location can influence economic opportunities and access to resources. Geographic differences may reflect historical institutions, infrastructure, natural conditions, market access, public investment, or differences in local economic activity. Studying these patterns requires both economic analysis and careful attention to geography.

title: Panchayat Libraries in Karnataka
content: Panchayat Libraries in Karnataka: Field Notes from AnekalField ImmersionAzim Premji Foundation, Bengaluru Urban, KarnatakaDecember 2024Supervisor: Prof. Srishti Yadav (Azim Premji University, Bengaluru)FieldworkI conducted 30 semi-structured informal interviews with key village stakeholders, including the Panchayat Development Officer, ward members, ASHA workers and Anganwadi workers, to understand government service delivery systems.I independently designed the interview questionnaire and conducted an in-depth interview with the Panchayat librarian. The fieldwork provided a ground-level understanding of the functioning of Panchayat libraries and their role in the community, and informed a report on the establishment, administration, financial structure, monitoring, and current functioning of Panchayat libraries in Karnataka.The fieldwork focused particularly on the Gram Panchayat Library at Neriga in Anekal taluk. The interview with the librarian provided information on library resources, procurement, financial constraints, administrative procedures, infrastructure, visitor records, educational demand, and the role of the library as a community space.Report insightsPanchayat libraries and rural knowledge infrastructureGram Panchayat Libraries form an important part of rural knowledge infrastructure, providing access to reading materials, public information, and learning spaces. They play a role in education, community development, and access to information, particularly in rural areas where access to educational resources can be more limited.The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the importance of these institutions. The closure of schools, colleges, and other educational institutions created additional barriers to educational resources for rural children. Children experienced disruptions in their learning routines and faced difficulties in accessing reading materials. During this period, libraries could provide an alternative source of educational materials and a space for students and other community members.The fieldwork at Neriga indicated a clear decline in regular study routines during the period of closures, followed by a gradual return after reopening. Demand for examination-related materials increased after schools reopened, although procurement of new materials did not always keep pace with this demand.Public library legislation in IndiaThe development of public libraries in India has largely taken place through state-level legislation. Tamil Nadu was among the earliest states to enact public library legislation with the Tamil Nadu Public Libraries Act of 1948, which was implemented in 1950. Andhra Pradesh followed with the Public Libraries Act in 1960, while Karnataka enacted its library legislation in 1965.Other states subsequently introduced public library legislation, including Maharashtra in 1967, West Bengal in 1979, Manipur, Haryana and Kerala in 1989, Mizoram and Goa in 1993, Odisha and Gujarat in 2001, Uttarakhand in 2005, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh in 2006, and Lakshadweep in 2007. Telangana’s public library legislation subsequently developed from the Andhra Pradesh Public Libraries Act following the reorganisation of Andhra Pradesh in 2014.These legislative developments reflect the role of state governments in establishing public library systems and expanding access to information, education, and literacy.The Karnataka Public Libraries Act, 1965The Karnataka Public Libraries Act, 1965 provided the legal foundation for establishing and maintaining a comprehensive public library service across the state. The Act came into effect in 1966 and supported the development of libraries across different administrative levels, including state, district, taluk, and Gram Panchayat levels.Karnataka became the third state in India to adopt a Library Act. The development of the state’s public library system was influenced by the work of Dr. S. R. Ranganathan, widely recognised as the Father of Library Science in India. The legislation provided the basis for expanding public library services across both rural and urban areas and aimed to promote equitable access to knowledge, education, and community development.The Act also required rural libraries to maintain a copy of the Constitution of India. The public library system developed as a hierarchical structure extending from the state level through district and taluk levels to Gram Panchayat libraries.In 1998, the Karnataka Public Libraries Act was amended to increase the annual grant for infrastructure development in district libraries from 3 percent to 6 percent of land revenue through the Karnataka Public Libraries (Amendment) Ordinance. The report also documents the extensive network of Gram Panchayat libraries that developed across the state.Transfer to Rural Development and Panchayat RajIn 2019, the management of rural libraries was transferred to the Department of Rural Development and Panchayat Raj (RDPR). Rural libraries were subsequently referred to as Gram Panchayat Library and Information Centres.The transfer brought library management closer to the local governance system and placed Gram Panchayats in a more direct position in relation to the administration and management of rural libraries. The transition affected funding, monitoring, administrative oversight, procurement, inspections, and the role of librarians.The post-2019 system also involved changes in administrative support, including regular salaries and inspections. At the local level, the fieldwork indicated that these changes were important in formalising administrative processes and providing greater institutional support to librarians.The RDPR system also promoted initiatives intended to encourage reading and community participation, including Oduva Belaku, Pustaka Jolige, Odina Manege Hogona, Ammanigagi Ondu Pustaka, Chaduranga Adona, and Chinnara Chittara Abhiyana.The fieldwork also indicated the presence of NGO-linked activities in Anekal through periodic reading events and limited infrastructure upgrades. However, day-to-day procurement of books and other resources remained constrained by local budgets and administrative processes.Financial devolutionThe report examines the role of library cess and other sources of funding in sustaining public libraries. Under the Karnataka Public Libraries Act, public libraries receive a share of property tax revenue collected by urban local bodies in the form of library cess. These resources are intended to support infrastructure, assets, books, subscriptions, and other library requirements.Before the 2019 transition, the allocation and administration of these resources were primarily handled by the Department of Public Libraries. Following the transfer of rural libraries to RDPR, Gram Panchayats became more directly involved in managing library resources and local expenditure.Public libraries are also supported through government grants, infrastructure and capacity-building resources, CSR contributions, donations, membership fees, revenue from services, local government allocations, and partnerships with educational institutions.The fieldwork at Neriga showed how these financial constraints affect everyday library functioning. Recurring requirements such as books, basic furniture, and small repairs compete within limited local budgets. Requests for new materials can require repeated administrative follow-up, while the absence of a dedicated resource officer can create an additional bottleneck in procurement.Monitoring and evaluationPublic libraries operate within a system of financial and administrative monitoring involving Gram Panchayats and RDPR. Libraries maintain records relating to visitors, expenditure, activities, and other aspects of their functioning. These records are submitted through the relevant Gram Panchayat and RDPR administrative channels.The report also documents the role of inspections and audits in maintaining administrative and financial accountability. At the local level, the fieldwork at Neriga indicated that the librarian maintained visitor and expenditure registers and that records were reviewed through the Panchayat and RDPR system.Annual audits and administrative oversight were part of the monitoring structure, while regular inspections and salary regularisation were identified as important post-2019 changes. These procedures influence the availability of resources, procurement processes, and the ability of libraries to respond to changing community needs.The Neriga Gram Panchayat LibraryThe fieldwork at the Neriga Gram Panchayat Library in Anekal taluk provided a detailed view of the everyday functioning of a rural library.The library housed approximately 11,000 books. However, a significant proportion of the collection consisted of older novels and textbooks. The librarian identified strong demand for updated educational resources, current textbooks, English storybooks, competitive examination guides, and multilingual content.The gap between the existing collection and community demand was an important issue. The library possessed a substantial number of books, but the usefulness of the collection depended on whether the available materials remained relevant to the needs of current users.The library also faced practical infrastructure constraints. Limited space and a shortage of study tables restricted the number of users that could be accommodated and affected the library’s ability to provide an effective study environment.Community demand and educational resourcesThe fieldwork suggested that demand for library resources is closely connected to the educational needs of the surrounding community. Current textbooks, competitive examination guides, children’s books, and English-language materials were identified as important areas of demand.The demand for examination-related materials was particularly relevant after the reopening of educational institutions. Students preparing for competitive examinations also required updated guides and study materials.These observations point to the importance of regularly updating library collections rather than relying primarily on older books. The usefulness of a rural library therefore depends not only on the size of its collection but also on the relevance, currency, and accessibility of the materials available to users.The fieldwork also highlighted the importance of basic physical infrastructure. Limited space and insufficient study tables constrained the ability of the library to function as a regular study and learning environment.Community engagementThe report also considers the role of Panchayat libraries as community spaces rather than simply repositories of books.The fieldwork highlighted possibilities for activities such as storytelling sessions, digital literacy programmes, personality development workshops, and cultural events. Such activities could increase regular participation and strengthen the library’s role as a shared community institution.Community engagement can also help libraries respond to local educational and informational needs. Activities aimed at children, students, and young people preparing for examinations could provide additional reasons for regular library use.The fieldwork suggested that rebuilding regular footfall requires attention not only to books and infrastructure but also to the activities and services that make the library relevant to the surrounding community.Key field observationThe field immersion connected the formal institutional structure of Panchayat libraries with their day-to-day functioning at the local level.The experience showed how funding, procurement, infrastructure, educational demand, administrative procedures, and community participation interact in shaping the functioning of a rural library.The Neriga fieldwork also illustrated the difference between having a formal institutional structure and having the resources required for that structure to function effectively. The library had a substantial collection and an established administrative system, but continued to face constraints related to updated materials, procurement, space, furniture, and community engagement.The fieldwork therefore provided a practical perspective on the functioning and community role of Panchayat libraries within Karnataka’s broader public library system. It also highlighted the importance of linking administrative reforms and financial devolution with the everyday needs of librarians and library users.
